blocks.text: A valve body has an internal passage that turns through a bend. In the ordinary front view it is a maze of dashed lines that nobody can read; cut the part along its centreline on paper and the passage is suddenly obvious.

blocks.markdown: Two problems recur in orthographic drawing. First, **internal features** (bores, cavities, passages) produce many hidden lines and become unreadable. Second, an **inclined face** appears foreshortened in the standard views, so its true size and shape cannot be read. **Sectional views** solve the first problem and **auxiliary views** solve the second.

blocks.title: Section view
blocks.text: A view obtained by imagining the part cut by a **cutting plane** and the nearer portion removed. The surfaces actually cut by the plane are shown with **hatching**. The cutting plane is marked on another view by a thick-ended chain line with arrows showing the viewing direction and letters (A-A), repeated above the section.

blocks.markdown: **Full section and hatching.** A **full section** passes the cutting plane through the whole part. Hatching conventions: thin continuous lines at **45 degrees** to the outline; evenly spaced (typically 2 to 4 mm apart, scaled to the area); **the same angle and spacing across one part**; where two adjacent parts are cut, the hatching of one runs the **opposite way** (or at a different spacing) from the other so they are distinguishable. Hatching stops at visible outlines, and hidden lines are normally omitted in a section.

rows: Chain, thick at ends, with arrows and letters
blocks.caption: Hatching and section marking

blocks.markdown: **Features not sectioned by convention.** Cutting through some parts would make the view misleading, because hatching would suggest a thicker, solid mass. By convention, items cut **lengthwise** (along their axis, or in the plane of their thin dimension) are left **unhatched**: solid shafts, bolts, nuts, screws, pins, rivets, keys, **ribs and webs** and spokes. They are sectioned (hatched) when cut **across** their axis or thickness.

blocks.title: Which items are hatched?
blocks.prompt: A pillow-block assembly is cut along the shaft axis by a vertical plane. The cut passes through the housing, the shaft, the outer ring of a bearing, a bolt and a stiffening rib of the housing that lies in the cutting plane. Which are hatched?

steps.text: Housing and bearing outer ring are solid material cut by the plane, so they are hatched; because they are adjacent parts, hatch them in opposite directions.
The shaft and the bolt are cut lengthwise along their axes, so by convention they are shown unhatched.
The rib lies in the cutting plane along its length, so it is not hatched either.

blocks.answer: Hatched: housing and bearing ring (opposite directions). Not hatched: shaft, bolt and rib.

blocks.markdown: **Auxiliary views.** A face inclined to the principal planes is shown at its **true shape** only when viewed along its normal. An auxiliary view is projected perpendicular to the inclined edge (not to the main view), with the distances from the fold line measured from the adjacent view. True length of an inclined edge with horizontal run $x$ and vertical rise $y$:

blocks.caption: True length of an inclined edge with run x and rise y (mm)

blocks.title: True shape of an inclined face
blocks.prompt: A rectangular ramp face rises 30 mm over a horizontal run of 40 mm and is 35 mm wide (the edge perpendicular to the slope). Find the true length and the true area of the face.

steps.text: True length of the slope edge.
The width is not foreshortened because it is parallel to the viewing plane: 35 mm.
True area, the product of the two true sides.

blocks.answer: True length 50 mm; true area 1750 mm^2, whereas the plan view shows only 40 x 35 = 1400 mm^2.

blocks.title: Never hatch a lengthwise cut shaft
blocks.text: Hatching a solid shaft or bolt cut lengthwise makes it look like a hollow or thick section, and standard practice is to leave it unhatched.

items: Choose the cutting plane through the features that need explaining.
Mark the plane on the view with arrows and letters.
Draw the section and hatch only the cut material at 45 degrees.
Leave lengthwise-cut ribs, shafts and fasteners unhatched.
For inclined faces, project an auxiliary view along the face normal.

points: A full section reveals internal features; hatching is thin 45-degree lines, even spacing, opposite directions for adjacent parts.
Shafts, bolts, keys and ribs cut lengthwise are not hatched.
An auxiliary view shows the true shape of an inclined face; true length = sqrt(run^2 + rise^2).

questions.stem: At what angle and in what line type is standard hatching drawn?
questions.explanation: Hatching uses thin continuous lines at 45 degrees to the outline. Thick lines are for outlines and dashes for hidden detail.

questions.stem: Which of these is normally left unhatched when cut lengthwise by a section plane?
questions.explanation: By convention solid shafts, bolts, keys and ribs cut lengthwise are not hatched. Housings, plates and covers are material and are hatched.

questions.stem: An inclined face has a horizontal run of 70 mm and a vertical rise of 24 mm. Calculate the true length of its slope edge, in mm.
questions.explanation: True length is sqrt(70^2 + 24^2) = sqrt(5476) = 74 mm. The plan or front view would show only 70 mm.

questions.stem: A rectangular inclined face has a slope edge with horizontal run 60 mm and rise 25 mm, and is 40 mm wide perpendicular to the slope. Calculate its true area in mm^2.
questions.explanation: True slope length is sqrt(60^2 + 25^2) = sqrt(4225) = 65 mm, so area is 65 x 40 = 2600 mm^2. A plan view would show only 60 x 40 = 2400 mm^2.

questions.stem: Two adjacent parts are cut by the same section plane in an assembly. How should they be hatched?

options.text: In opposite directions or with different spacing

questions.correctOptionText: In opposite directions or with different spacing
questions.explanation: Different directions or spacing let the eye separate the two parts, which can otherwise look like one solid. Using the same direction would merge the two parts visually.

questions.stem: A section plane passes along the length of a bolt in an assembly. How is the bolt shown in the section?

options.text: Hatched in the opposite direction to its neighbours

questions.explanation: Fasteners cut lengthwise are shown unhatched by convention. Hatching would suggest a larger solid mass than the bolt really is.

questions.stem: A cutting plane first passes through the centre of a stiffening rib along its length, and a second plane passes across the rib at right angles to its length. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The rib is hatched in both
The rib is unhatched in the first section and hatched in the second
The rib is hatched in the first and unhatched in the second
The rib is unhatched in both

questions.correctOptionText: The rib is unhatched in the first section and hatched in the second
questions.explanation: A rib cut lengthwise is left unhatched, since hatching would suggest it is as thick as the base. When cut across, its section is a true area of material and is hatched.

questions.stem: Describe how to construct a full section view and hatch it correctly, referring to the cutting plane line, hatching and hidden lines.
markingGuide: Mark the cutting plane with chain line, thick ends, arrows and letters
Remove the near portion and draw the cut view
Hatch cut material at 45 degrees, thin, evenly spaced
Normally omit hidden lines in the section
questions.explanation: The answer must include labelling, hatching rules and the treatment of hidden lines. Each point in the marking guide earns credit, so state every point explicitly and give its reason.

questions.stem: A part has a face inclined at 35 degrees to the horizontal. Explain how to construct an auxiliary view showing its true shape and why the standard views do not.
markingGuide: Standard views foreshorten by the cosine of the angle
Project perpendicular to the inclined edge, parallel to the face normal
Transfer widths from the adjacent view using the fold line
Draw the true length edge and the true width
questions.explanation: Credit for the reason (foreshortening) and the method (projection along the face normal). Each point in the marking guide earns credit, so state every point explicitly and give its reason.

questions.stem: An auxiliary view that shows the true shape of an inclined face is obtained by looking along the normal to that face.
questions.explanation: Only when the line of sight is perpendicular to the face is nothing foreshortened. The principal views look along other directions and so shorten the face.
